prompt: What is the difference between a one-shot and a few-shot prompt?

choices.text: One solved example in the prompt, against several
choices.why: Right. Zero-shot has none, one-shot one, few-shot several.

choices.text: One attempt at the answer against several
choices.why: The number of attempts is unrelated. It is about examples inside the prompt.

choices.text: One sentence of instruction against several
choices.why: Instructions can be any length in either. The examples are what is counted.

choices.text: A single model against several models voting
choices.why: Several models voting is another technique, lesson 27. Few-shot is one prompt with examples.

prompt: Why did `toylm generate "question : is the bread fresh ? answer :"` reply `yes.` when nothing told it to answer?
hint: What does a model do with the text in front of it?

choices.text: It understood that a question had been asked
choices.why: It counted which words follow `answer :`. No understanding was needed.

choices.text: Temperature 0 makes models answer questions
choices.why: Temperature 0 picks the top score. The pattern decided what the top score was.

choices.text: It searched its corpus for the bread's freshness
choices.why: It has no search. It has counts of which word follows which pair.

choices.text: The pattern made a reply likeliest
choices.why: Right. It continues the pattern, and in its corpus `answer :` is followed by an answer.

prompt: `toylm` answered `yes.` to `question : when does the café open ? answer :`. What does its context line explain?
hint: Which two words did it look at?

choices.text: The café opens at a time of yes
choices.why: The corpus says seven. The question never reached the model.

choices.text: The corpus has no answer about opening times
choices.why: It has `answer : at seven` after that question. The model could not see the question.

choices.text: Only the last two words were visible to it
choices.why: Right. With a two-word view the question was out of sight, so it took the format from the pattern and none of the content.

choices.text: It picked the answer at random
choices.why: Temperature 0 picks the top score; `yes` has 50% after `answer :`.

prompt: After `answer :`, what percentage did `toylm next` give `yes`?
hint: The first row of the table.

prompt: What does the toy's failure on the opening-hours question show about few-shot examples in a large model?

choices.text: Large models also see only the last two words
choices.why: A large model sees the whole prompt. The toy's view is an exaggeration that makes the split visible.

choices.text: Examples fix the form; the input decides the content
choices.why: Right. A pattern is strong at format and boundary, and guarantees nothing about whether the answer is right.

choices.text: Few-shot prompts produce wrong content more often than zero-shot ones
choices.why: The lesson made no such claim. It said examples do not guarantee content.

choices.text: Examples are useless for questions with times as answers
choices.why: They fix the form of such answers well. The toy failed because it cannot see the question.

prompt: Lesson 20's strong prompt described sarcasm and still missed `r5`. Why can a few-shot version do better?

choices.text: It shows the sarcastic case on the right side
choices.why: Right. An example shows where the boundary falls, which a description only tells.

choices.text: Examples make the model more intelligent
choices.why: A prompt changes nothing in the model. It changes what is likely to come next.

choices.text: Examples are read before the instructions
choices.why: Order matters, but that is not why. The example carries information the description did not.

choices.text: A few-shot prompt is sent at a lower temperature
choices.why: Temperature is a separate setting, chosen independently of the prompt.

prompt: A one-shot prompt's single example is labelled `not_a_review`. What risk does the lesson name?
hint: With one example, what looks like part of the pattern?

choices.text: The model will refuse to use other labels
choices.why: It can use them; the example makes one label look more likely, not the others impossible.

choices.text: The example will be deleted from the prompt
choices.why: Nothing removes it. It is sent with every request.

choices.text: Nothing, since one example is enough to show the format
choices.why: It shows the format and also biases the label, which is the risk.

choices.text: It tilts the model towards `not_a_review`
choices.why: Right. With one example, its label, length and topic all look like the pattern.

prompt: Why does the café's few-shot prompt have one example of each of the four labels?

choices.text: Because a prompt is limited to four examples
choices.why: There is no such limit. Each example costs tokens, which is a reason to keep few, not a rule of four.

choices.text: Because the model needs to see each label to know it exists
choices.why: The labels are listed in the instructions. The examples show where each one applies.

choices.text: So that no label looks like the default
choices.why: Right. Covering and balancing the classes keeps the examples from teaching a favourite.

choices.text: To make the prompt the same length as the test set
choices.why: The test set has eight messages, and its length is unrelated to the examples.

prompt: Why is the sarcastic message the FIRST example rather than the last?

choices.text: Models only read the first example they are given
choices.why: They read all of them. Position matters at the margin, not absolutely.

choices.text: Sarcasm must always come first in a prompt
choices.why: There is no such rule. The point is not to let position teach anything.

choices.text: The last example's label has an easy route into the next answer
choices.why: Right. Varying the order keeps the hard case, and its label, from sitting next to the message being labelled.

choices.text: The examples have to be in alphabetical order
choices.why: `negative`, `not_a_review`, `mixed`, `positive` is not alphabetical, and that is fine.

prompt: Someone takes `r1` to `r8` from lesson 20's test set as the few-shot examples. What goes wrong?

choices.text: The prompt becomes too long to send
choices.why: It becomes longer and costlier, but that is not the main problem.

choices.text: The test then checks answers it contains
choices.why: Right. A score of 8 of 8 would measure memory, not labelling, and new messages would be untested.

choices.text: The model refuses repeated messages
choices.why: Nothing refuses them. The problem is the measurement, not the model.

choices.text: The labels in the test set are wrong
choices.why: They were decided by a person. Using them as examples is the problem, not their accuracy.

prompt: How many tokens did `tok count` give for `prompt-few.txt`?
At the illustrative prices, what did `tok cost` give for 10,000 requests with `prompt-few.txt`?
hint: The last line of the second `tok cost`.

prompt: Why are a prompt's examples paid for on every request?

choices.text: Providers charge a fee for each example
choices.why: There is no fee per example. They are input tokens like any others.

choices.text: The model retrains on them at each request
choices.why: Nothing is retrained. They are read as input, every time.

choices.text: They are only paid for once
choices.why: Each request is independent, and the examples are input in each.

choices.text: Everything is sent again each time
choices.why: Right. Nothing is remembered between requests, so the examples travel with every one.

prompt: Which of these would make the café's few-shot examples worse? Choose all that apply.
hint: Check each against the five rules and the format.

choices.text: Three `negative` examples and one `positive`
choices.why: Yes: unbalanced labels make `negative` look like the usual answer.

choices.text: An example answered `Negative (sarcastic)`
choices.why: Yes: it contradicts the stated output format, leaving two signals that disagree.

choices.text: A Portuguese message among the examples
choices.why: It shows that messages in other languages get English labels, which is wanted.

choices.text: Four examples that are all short and easy
choices.why: Yes: they teach short and easy, and nothing about the hard cases.

prompt: Because examples cost tokens on every request, you stop adding them when the ___ set stops improving.
hint: What lesson 20 used to count right answers.

prompt: Put the work of adding examples to a prompt in order.
items: Score the zero-shot prompt on the test set
Read which kind of failure remains
Add an example that shows that boundary
Score again and keep it only if the count moves

prompt: Match each prompt to how many solved examples it holds.
A few-shot prompt now labels every sarcastic test message correctly, and also labels two plain positive reviews `negative`. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: What did the examples have in common?

choices.text: The model has learnt sarcasm permanently
choices.why: A prompt teaches nothing permanent. The examples tilt each reply.

choices.text: The tokenizer split the reviews wrongly
choices.why: Token boundaries do not flip a positive review to negative.

choices.text: The test set labels are wrong
choices.why: Two plain positive reviews were labelled correctly before. The prompt changed, not the labels.

choices.text: The examples tilt towards `negative`
choices.why: Right. Too many negative or sarcastic examples tilt the pattern; rebalance and score again.
